summary: Specifies how to carry Adaptive Multi-Rate (AMR) and Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband (AMR-WB) encoded speech in RTP packets. It is designed to interoperate with existing AMR transport formats on non-IP networks, and it also defines a file format for storing AMR speech. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Phone voices are squeezed into small codes. This note says how to put those codes into network packets, and how to save them in a file.

subtitle: How to pack AMR and AMR-WB speech into RTP packets, and how to store it in files.

tldr.problem: The AMR and AMR-WB speech codecs were designed for circuit-switched mobile radio, but they are also wanted for real-time speech over packet networks such as the Internet, and gateways must connect the two worlds.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload carries a small header with a codec mode request, a table of contents with one entry per speech frame, and then the speech data. Two layouts exist, bandwidth-efficient and octet-aligned, and the octet-aligned one adds optional frame CRCs, robust sorting and interleaving.
tldr.outcome: It also defines a simple file format and two media type registrations, one for AMR and one for AMR-WB. It obsoletes RFC 3267 and adds offer/answer rules for negotiating the options.

facts.value: 8 bits, polynomial 1 + x^2 + x^3 + x^4 + x^8

sections.title: Two Codecs, One Payload Format
sections.content:
RFC 4867 specifies how to packetize AMR (Adaptive Multi-Rate) and AMR-WB (Adaptive Multi-Rate Wideband) encoded speech into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). The format supports several channels, several frames per payload, fast codec mode adaptation, robustness against packet loss and bit errors, and interoperation with existing AMR transport formats on non-IP networks.

The document also defines a file format for storage uses such as email, and it includes two media type registrations. It obsoletes RFC 3267 and adds offer/answer rules. AMR and AMR-WB are different codecs and are always handled as different RTP payload types.
sections.eli5: Two kinds of voice codes need a way to travel in network packets. This document is the packing list for both, plus a way to keep them in a file.

sections.title: How AMR and AMR-WB Behave
sections.content:
AMR supports eight narrow band encoding modes with bit rates between 4.75 and 12.2 kbps. It samples at 8000 Hz and encodes 20 ms frames, so each frame stands for 160 samples. AMR-WB supports nine wide band modes from 6.6 to 23.85 kbps, samples at 16000 Hz and uses 20 ms frames of 320 samples.

Both are multi-mode codecs. The receiver can ask the sender to change mode with a Codec Mode Request (CMR) that rides along on frames going the other way, so no separate signalling is needed. Both also support voice activity detection and comfort noise: during silence the sender may send only Silence Indicator (SID) frames.

The speech bits in a frame are not equally sensitive to errors. They are split into classes A, B and C, with class A the most sensitive. A frame is only declared damaged if class A bits are corrupted, and a damaged frame can still help error concealment. The RFC copies the AMR class A sizes into a table (Table 1) to make them normative for this payload format.

Several frames that cover the same 20 ms in a multi-channel session form a frame-block. In an N-channel session a frame-block holds N frames, one per channel.

For robustness against packet loss the sender can resend earlier frame-blocks in later packets, in the same or a lower mode. This needs no signalling, and a receiver that gets several versions of a frame is advised to use the highest rate one. The RFC says RFC 2198 is only indicated when the spread between primary and redundant data exceeds 5 frames or a non-AMR codec is wanted for the redundancy.
sections.eli5: The codec chops talking into 20 millisecond slices and can use a bigger or smaller code for each slice. The listener can ask for a different size, like asking someone to speak up or speak softly.

sections.title: Bandwidth-Efficient Mode
sections.content:
An RTP payload has a payload header, a table of contents (ToC) and speech data. The RTP timestamp counts samples, so it grows by 160 for AMR and 320 for AMR-WB per frame-block. The marker bit is set to 1 when the first frame-block in the packet is the first of a talkspurt.

In bandwidth-efficient mode the payload header is just the 4-bit CMR. Its value is the frame type index of the requested mode, and 15 means no request. A terminal with no preference SHOULD send 15. The CMR MUST be 15 for packets sent to a multicast group, and an IP endpoint SHOULD NOT set the CMR based on packet loss or congestion.

Each ToC entry has 6 bits: an F bit (1 means another frame follows), a 4-bit FT frame type and a Q quality bit (0 means severely damaged). FT=15 is NO_DATA and, for AMR-WB, FT=14 is SPEECH_LOST; neither has speech bits in the payload. A packet with an FT of 9 to 14 for AMR, or 10 to 13 for AMR-WB, SHOULD be discarded entirely. With N channels and K frame-blocks there MUST be N*K ToC entries.

The whole payload is packed bit by bit and padded with 0 to 7 zero bits to reach an octet boundary.
sections.eli5: Each speech slice gets a tiny label saying how big it is and whether it is good or damaged. Everything is squeezed together with almost no wasted space, like packing a suitcase tightly.

sections.title: Octet-Aligned Mode and Its Options
sections.content:
In octet-aligned mode every field starts on an octet boundary. The payload header is the 4-bit CMR plus four reserved bits that MUST be zero. Each ToC entry is one octet (F, FT, Q and two zero padding bits), and the last octet of each speech frame is padded with zeros. Only this mode can use the three robustness options below.

  • Frame CRC: an optional list of 8-bit CRCs, one per speech frame, computed over the class A bits only with the generator polynomial 1 + x^2 + x^3 + x^4 + x^8. A mismatch means the receiver MUST clear the Q bit, so the frame is treated as damaged.
  • Robust sorting: the octets of all frames in a payload are interleaved at octet level, so the most sensitive bits sit near the front of the packet where partial-checksum or error-protection schemes can cover them.
  • Frame-block interleaving: two extra 4-bit fields, ILL and ILP, follow the CMR. An interleaving length of ILL+1 spreads consecutive frame-blocks over several packets so that a lost packet costs scattered single frame-blocks rather than a burst. All packets in a group MUST use the same ILL and carry the same number of frame-blocks.

No operating mode is mandatory. An implementation SHOULD support both bandwidth-efficient and octet-aligned mode for a single channel, while interleaving, robust sorting and CRCs are optional. A receiver SHOULD discard a packet whose length does not match what its headers imply.
sections.eli5: In this mode every item sits in its own whole box, which wastes a little space but is easy to handle. It also allows extras like a second check number and shuffling, so one lost packet does not wipe out a whole word.

sections.title: The Storage Format
sections.content:
The storage format keeps AMR or AMR-WB frames in a file or an email attachment. A file is a header followed by speech frames. Single-channel files use only a magic number, and multi-channel files add a 32-bit channel description field whose low 4 bits (CHAN) give the number of channels.

After the header, frame-blocks follow in time order. Each stored frame starts with a one-octet header holding the FT and Q fields, then the speech bits, zero-padded to an octet boundary. Frames not received between SID updates MUST be stored as NO_DATA (frame type 15), and lost ones as NO_DATA or SPEECH_LOST (type 14, AMR-WB only), in complete frame-blocks to stay in sync with the original media. For needs such as random access or synchronization with video, the RFC points to the 3GP file format instead.
sections.eli5: Saving to a file is like keeping the same labelled slices in a row inside a folder. The first line of the file tells you which kind of codes follow.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters and SDP
sections.content:
Options are agreed out of band through parameters in the audio/AMR and audio/AMR-WB media type registrations, which RFC 4867 defines. They include octet-align, mode-set, mode-change-period, mode-change-capability, mode-change-neighbor, maxptime, crc, robust-sorting, interleaving, channels and max-red. Setting crc, robust-sorting or interleaving implies octet-aligned operation.

In SDP the RTP clock rate in a=rtpmap MUST be 8000 for AMR and 16000 for AMR-WB, and the remaining parameters go in a=fmtp. In offer/answer, the answerer MUST return octet-align, crc, robust-sorting, interleaving and channels unmodified or drop the payload type. A mode-set in an offer must come back unmodified or the payload type is rejected. max-red, between 0 and 65535 ms, bounds how far apart a frame and its redundant copy can be sent.

The mode change parameters exist for gateways to GSM networks. Encoders SHOULD change mode only to neighboring modes and in multiples of 40 ms (two frame-blocks), while decoders SHOULD accept changes at any time.
sections.eli5: Before talking, both sides agree on settings, like choosing which language and how fast to speak. These parameters are the list of settings they can pick.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Security
sections.content:
The general RTP congestion rules apply. The multi-rate design helps, since switching mode changes the bandwidth demand, and so does packing more frame-blocks per packet, at the cost of delay. Any redundancy added to fight loss must itself be regulated. Applications SHOULD employ congestion control, for example something like TCP Friendly Rate Control.

The payload format has no built-in security. The RFC lists confidentiality, authentication and integrity of the speech as the main issues, and recommends external mechanisms, with SRTP preferred and IPsec and TLS as other options. Encryption should happen after packetization, and key changes should fall at the boundary between interleaving groups. Using error-tolerant tricks such as robust sorting can be hard to combine with encryption or integrity checks, since any bit error makes an integrity check fail. Tampering with the CMR can change the speech quality.
sections.eli5: The packets themselves are like postcards that anyone can read. To keep a call private you must put them in a locked envelope, which is a separate tool.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3267
sections.content: This RFC replaces RFC 3267. Its main changes are an offer/answer section, a new mode-change-capability parameter that defaults to 1, restricting mode-change-period to 1 or 2, making mode-change-neighbor a recommendation rather than a requirement, and adding the max-red parameter so a receiver knows whether redundancy is used. It also aligns the unequal error detection text with the published UDP-Lite specification, clarifies the CRC bit order and padding bits, forbids comfort noise frame types 9, 10 and 11 in the AMR file format, and clarifies how encryption and integrity protection apply to the payload.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up second edition of an earlier note, with fixes for the parts people found confusing and a few new settings.
